pos: n. (d. 1584; Bishop of Kildare under Edward VI, deprived under Mary, and Archbishop of Armagh from 1568)
etymology: Lancaster, an English surname from the city on the Lune; Lune, the river, and Old English caster, from Latin castrum, a fort.
biblical_def: Thomas Lancaster was an Englishman and a convinced Protestant whose career tracks the whole of the Tudor religious reversal. Made Bishop of Kildare in 1549, he was consecrated by the new English ordinal, pressed the Prayer Book, married, and was deprived under Mary in 1554 for both his doctrine and his wife. He spent the Marian years in exile and in English parishes, returned under Elizabeth, and in 1568 was appointed Archbishop of Armagh, which he held until his death in 1584. He was one of the few archbishops of the period who actually tried to get preaching into the Irish parishes, repeatedly reporting to Dublin and London that there were neither ministers nor churches nor funds, and getting very little. The dictionary records him for the pattern of a ministry conducted across reversals: “But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to deprive as to divest of an office or dignity; an evangelist as a preacher of the gospel, one who declares good tidings; and reproach as censure mingled with contempt, shame.
webster_full: DEPRIVE, v.t. [L. deprivo.] To take from; to hinder from possessing or enjoying; to divest of an ecclesiastical preferment or office.
EVANGELIST, n. [Gr. euaggelistes.] A writer of the history of Jesus Christ; a preacher of the gospel; one who declares good tidings.
REPROACH, n. Censure mingled with contempt; abuse; shame; infamy; that which is the cause of shame.
ORDINAL, n. A book containing the order of divine service, especially the form of making and consecrating ministers.
PARTAKER, n. One who has or takes a part, share or portion in common with others.
scriptures: But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God;
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach.
Act 5:41
And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Kildare from 1549, deprived under Mary for his doctrine and his marriage, and Archbishop of Armagh from 1568 to 1584, pressing fruitlessly for preaching in the Irish parishes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a flattening of the Tudor bishops worth refusing, which treats them all as weathervanes who turned with each reign. Many did. Lancaster did not: he was deprived, exiled and restored, and his doctrine in 1568 was his doctrine of 1549. The dictionary notes the distinction because it matters for how the Irish failure is explained. Armagh under Lancaster was not a see in the hands of a trimmer; it was a see in the hands of a reformer with no money, no clergy and no Irish.

The principle to recover is that endurance across reversals is part of the charge rather than an interruption of it. Paul's last charge to Timothy puts affliction inside the job description: “But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5), and the shame attached to it is to be owned rather than avoided — “Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner” (2Ti 1:8). Hebrews calls the reader outside the camp to bear reproach with Christ (Heb 13:13), and the apostles treat that reproach as an honour conferred (Act 5:41).

“Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord” (2Ti 1:8) — deprived for his doctrine and for his marriage.
“rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name” (Act 5:41) — his doctrine in 1568 was his doctrine of 1549.

pos: n. (1527–1595; Irish-born Archbishop of Armagh, one of the few native Protestant bishops of the period)
etymology: Garvey, from Irish O Gairbhith, descendant of Garbhith, rough peace; garbh, rough, and sith, peace.
biblical_def: John Garvey was born in County Mayo, educated at Oxford, and was one of the very small number of Irishmen who took orders in the reformed Church of Ireland and rose in it. He was Dean of Ferns, then Dean of Christ Church Dublin from 1565, Bishop of Kilmore from 1585, and Archbishop of Armagh from 1589 until his death in 1595. He spoke Irish, which almost none of his episcopal colleagues did, and he sat on the commissions that governed the country as well as the church. He was by the standards of the Irish establishment a conscientious administrator rather than a great preacher. The dictionary records him because a native minister bears a particular grief for his own people, and Paul put it in words no Englishman in Ireland could have written: “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom 9:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a kinsman as a man of the same race or family; a dean as an ecclesiastical dignitary presiding over a cathedral chapter; and desire as an emotion directed to the attainment of some object.
webster_full: KINSMAN, n. A man of the same race or family; one related by blood.
DEAN, n. [L. decanus.] An ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral churches, the head of the chapter.
DESIRE, n. An emotion or excitement of the mind, directed to the attainment or possession of an object.
ACCURSED, participle passive. Doomed to destruction or misery; separated; devoted to destruction.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and speech; a language, the speech of a nation.
scriptures: Rom 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Rom 10:1
Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
Jer 9:1
Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!
And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,
corruption_summary: Irish-born Archbishop of Armagh from 1589, an Irish speaker and one of the very few natives to rise in the reformed Church of Ireland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Garvey's rarity is the point of his entry and is an indictment rather than a compliment. A reformed church in Ireland staffed almost entirely from England, in a country that mostly did not speak English, had made a decision about whose church it was. Garvey's career shows that native Irishmen could and did serve it, and that the establishment nevertheless did not go looking for them in anything like the numbers that would have made a difference.

The principle to recover is the particular burden a man carries for his own nation, which Scripture treats as proper and intense rather than as parochial. Paul's is extreme and sincere: “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom 9:3), and he states the content of it plainly — “my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved” (Rom 10:1). Jeremiah weeps for the daughter of his people (Jer 9:1). And when Paul addresses that people he does it in their own tongue, and the crowd falls silent to hear it (Act 21:40).

“he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue” (Act 21:40) — almost none of his episcopal colleagues had the Irish language.

pos: n. (c. 1523–1622; Archbishop of Cashel for fifty-one years and the worst pluralist of the Irish Reformation)
etymology: Magrath, from Irish Mac Graith, son of Craith; Miler, an Irish form of the Norman Milo.
biblical_def: Miler Magrath was a Fermanagh man, a Franciscan, whom Rome appointed Bishop of Down and Connor in 1565. Within two years he had conformed to the Church of Ireland and been given Clogher by the crown, and in 1571 Cashel, which he held for fifty-one years until his death in 1622. He accumulated the sees of Waterford and Lismore and Killala and Achonry at various times, something over seventy benefices, and for a period held appointments from both Rome and the crown at once; the churches in his gift went unserved while the revenues came in. He died at ninety-nine and lies in Cashel cathedral under an epitaph of his own composition. The dictionary records him because Malachi's complaint is exactly the case: “Who is there even among you that would shut the doors for nought?” (Mal 1:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lucre as gain in money, sordid gain; hire as the price paid for labour or service; and to corrupt as to vitiate, to pervert, to spoil.
webster_full: LUCRE, n. [L. lucrum.] Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base or unworthy.
HIRE, n. The price, reward or compensation paid for personal service, or for the use of a thing.
CORRUPT, v.t. [L. corrumpo.] To vitiate or deprave; to change from good to bad; to pervert; to spoil.
PLURALIST, n. A clerk or clergyman who holds more ecclesiastical benefices than one, with cure of souls.
COVETOUS, a. Inordinately desirous; excessively eager to obtain and possess; avaricious.
scriptures: Mal 1:10

Who is there even among you that would shut the doors for nought? neither do ye kindle fire on mine altar for nought. I have no pleasure in you, saith the LORD of hosts, neither will I accept an offering at your hand.
Mal 2:8
But ye are departed out of the way; ye have caused many to stumble at the law; ye have corrupted the covenant of Levi, saith the LORD of hosts.
Mic 3:11

The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous;
corruption_summary: Archbishop of Cashel from 1571 to 1622, who held sees from both Rome and the crown, accumulated four dioceses and over seventy benefices, and left the churches unserved.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption in this entry is the man, and it belongs to the Protestant side of the account. Magrath was not an enemy of the Reformation placed in Cashel to obstruct it; he was the crown's own choice, confirmed and reconfirmed, protected by Elizabeth personally against repeated complaints from Irish officials who knew exactly what he was doing. The dictionary names the protection as well as the man, because a government that knowingly keeps such a figure in a metropolitan see for half a century has told the country what it thinks the gospel is worth.

The principle to recover is that revenue taken for a ministry not performed is named in Scripture as contempt of God rather than mere laziness. Malachi's sarcasm is about priests who will not so much as shut a door without pay: “Who is there even among you that would shut the doors for nought?” (Mal 1:10). The charge is that they have corrupted a covenant and caused many to stumble (Mal 2:8). Micah describes a whole leadership class on commission — “and the priests thereof teach for hire” (Mic 3:11) — and Paul disqualifies from the office any man “greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:3).

Greek aischrokerdes (G146) — eager for base gain, greedy of filthy lucre; 1 Timothy 3:3.

“not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:3) — the churches in his gift went unserved while the revenues came in.

pos: n. (c. 1559–1633; Bishop of the Isles and then of Raphoe, who ordained Scottish Presbyterians on their own terms)
etymology: Knox, a Scottish surname from Old English cnocc, a hillock; Andrew, from Greek andreios, manly.
biblical_def: Andrew Knox was a Scot, minister of Paisley and then Bishop of the Isles, who was given the Irish see of Raphoe in 1611 and held both until 1619, when he kept Raphoe alone. East Donegal had filled with Scottish Presbyterian settlers under the Plantation of Ulster, and Knox staffed their parishes by ordaining Scottish ministers on a modified subscription: a man could state his scruples about the ceremonies and the surplice and be ordained anyway, sometimes with Presbyterian ministers laying on hands alongside the bishop. For a generation Ulster had a settled Scots ministry inside the established church. Wentworth and Bramhall broke the arrangement in the 1630s by requiring full conformity, and Ulster Presbyterianism went its own way. The dictionary records him for what the apostles did at Jerusalem: “Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God” (Act 15:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to edify as to instruct and improve the mind in knowledge or in morals; offence as that which causes stumbling or scruple; and a sentence as a judgment pronounced, an opinion given.
webster_full: EDIFY, v.t. [L. aedifico.] To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge generally, and particularly in moral and religious knowledge.
OFFENCE, n. [L. offensio.] A stumbling block; cause of stumbling or scruple; any transgression of law.
SENTENCE, n. [L. sententia.] An opinion; a judgment pronounced; a maxim; a short saying containing moral instruction.
SCRUPLE, n. Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right or expedient.
SURPLICE, n. A white garment worn by clergymen of the established church over their other dress.
scriptures: Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God:
Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God:
Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
Rom 15:7
Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Raphoe from 1611, who ordained Scottish Presbyterian ministers on a modified subscription and gave Ulster a settled Scots ministry until the 1630s.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest criticism of Knox is that his formula was deliberately imprecise. Men received episcopal ordination while stating that they did not hold the office to be what the church held it to be, and both parties agreed not to press the point. That bought a generation of peace and a working ministry; it also left the real disagreement undefined, so that when Bramhall called the question in the 1630s there was no agreed ground to stand on and the breach was worse for the delay.

The principle to recover is nevertheless the one the apostles acted on, which is a strong presumption against adding burdens. James's ruling at Jerusalem is exactly that: “Wherefore my sentence is, that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God” (Act 15:19). Paul generalises it into a rule about giving offence in any direction — “Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God” (1Co 10:32) — and names the two tests by which such arrangements should be judged: “Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19).

“Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God” (1Co 10:32) — a settled Scots ministry inside the established church.
“things wherewith one may edify another” (Rom 14:19) — the arrangement broken by enforced conformity in the 1630s.

pos: n. (c. 1569–1621; Bishop of Derry, Raphoe and Clogher at once, the planter bishop of Ulster)
etymology: Montgomery, a Norman surname from Sainte-Foy-de-Montgommery; mont, a hill, and the personal name Gomeric.
biblical_def: George Montgomery was a Scot, James I's chaplain, who in 1605 was given the three Ulster sees of Derry, Raphoe and Clogher together, and from 1610 Meath as well. His work was the temporal recovery of the Ulster church: he rode the dioceses with surveyors and lawyers, established what church lands had been alienated during the wars, recovered a great deal of it, and secured the endowments on which the Ulster establishment afterwards lived. He also, like Andrew Knox, took a soft line with the Scottish Presbyterian settlers and did not press conformity on them. His accumulation of sees was exactly the pluralism the dictionary condemns elsewhere, and he was at the same time one of the few bishops who made the Irish church solvent. The dictionary records the whole of that. “Then contended I with the rulers” is Nehemiah's word for the work (Neh 13:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to alienate as to transfer title or property to another; a portion as a part assigned, an allotment; and to rob as to take away by violence or wrong, to deprive unjustly.
webster_full: ALIENATE, v.t. [L. alieno.] To transfer title or property to another; to convey; to estrange.
PORTION, n. [L. portio.] A part of any thing separated from it; a part assigned; an allotment; a dividend.
ROB, v.t. To take from another by violence or wrong; to deprive unjustly; to plunder.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a church, charity or institution.
CONTEND, v.i. [L. contendo.] To strive in opposition; to struggle; to dispute earnestly.
scriptures: And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them: for the Levites and the singers, that did the work, were fled every one to his field.
Mal 3:8
Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.
Do ye not know that they which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple? and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar?
Hag 1:9

Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the LORD of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Derry, Raphoe and Clogher together from 1605 and of Meath from 1610, who recovered the alienated lands on which the Ulster church establishment afterwards lived.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry has to hold a tension the dictionary will not resolve by preference. Montgomery held three dioceses at once, and the case against pluralism made against Miler Magrath on this very page's neighbours applies to him too. What he did with the time is the difference: he recovered the church's stolen endowments and made it possible to pay ministers in Ulster at all. The defence is real, and it is still a defence of an abuse. A church that has to break its own rules to pay its clergy has a prior problem it is not solving.

The principle to recover is that the material support of the ministry is a spiritual matter and its neglect is theft. Nehemiah finds the Levites gone back to their farms because they had not been paid: “And I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them” (Neh 13:10). Malachi calls withholding by its name — “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me” (Mal 3:8). Paul argues the ministry's maintenance from the temple's own arrangements (1Co 9:13). And Haggai traces a nation's thin harvests to a house left waste while every man saw to his own (Hag 1:9).

pos: n. (1605–1682; Bishop of Clogher and then Meath, commissioner for the 1641 depositions and Cromwell's Scoutmaster-General)
etymology: Jones, a patronymic from John, Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Henry, from Old High German heim, home, and rih, ruler.
biblical_def: Henry Jones was a grandson of James Ussher's uncle, Dean of Kilmore and then of Clogher, and was in Ulster when the rising broke out in October 1641. He was taken prisoner by the insurgents, released, and sent to London, where parliament made him chief of the commission to take the sworn statements of the survivors. He became Bishop of Clogher in 1645, served as Scoutmaster-General — chief of intelligence — to Cromwell's army in Ireland, conformed again at the Restoration, and was Bishop of Meath from 1661 until his death in 1682. A bishop running an army's intelligence is a thing the dictionary records without approving. “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh” (2Co 10:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scoutmaster as the officer who commands the scouts of an army; to accuse falsely as to charge with a crime without ground; and to wrestle as to strive, to contend.
webster_full: SCOUT, n. A person sent before an army, or to a distance, for the purpose of observing the motions of an enemy.
ACCUSE, v.t. [L. accuso.] To charge with a crime, offense or fault; to blame; to censure.
WRESTLE, v.i. To strive with arms extended, as two men who seize each other; to struggle; to contend.
PRINCIPALITY, n. Sovereignty; a prince; one invested with sovereignty; a territory ruled by a prince.
CONTENT, a. Satisfied so as not to repine; easy in mind; quiet; not disturbed.
scriptures: For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh:
Eph 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Luk 3:14
And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
corruption_summary: Bishop of Clogher from 1645 and of Meath from 1661, chief commissioner for the 1641 depositions and Scoutmaster-General to Cromwell's army in Ireland.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary has two criticisms to make and both are of men on its own side of the Irish question. The first is the office: a bishop serving as an army's head of intelligence has confused two callings, whatever the justice of the war, and the New Testament's separation of the minister's weapons from the soldier's is not a technicality. The second is the use made of the depositions. Jones himself published a selection of them in 1642 as a pamphlet, with the framing and the arithmetic that made them propaganda, and the inflation of real crimes into fantastic totals helped justify what followed in 1649.

The principle to recover is that the minister's warfare is of a different order, stated plainly and without allowance for emergencies: “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh” (2Co 10:3), and the adversary is named as other than human: “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers” (Eph 6:12). John the Baptist does not tell soldiers to stop being soldiers; he tells them what righteousness requires of them as soldiers, including “neither accuse any falsely” (Luk 3:14). And a man taking sworn evidence is under James's rule about being swift to hear and slow to speak (Jas 1:19).

pos: n. (c. 1527–1584; Bishop of Meath, who reported the ruin of his diocese to a government that would not pay for it)
etymology: Brady, from Irish Mac Bradaigh, son of the spirited one; bradach, spirited or thieving.
biblical_def: Hugh Brady was an Irishman, educated at Oxford, and Bishop of Meath from 1563 until his death in 1584 — the largest and richest Irish diocese and the one nearest Dublin. He was a genuine Protestant and an energetic visitor, and the reports he sent to Dublin and to Cecil in London are among the most valuable documents of the Irish Reformation because they are honest. He counted the ruined churches: by his own survey well over a hundred parish churches in Meath were without roofs, and the great majority of the parishes had no preaching minister of any kind, many of them served by men who could not read English, let alone preach in Irish. He asked repeatedly for money and ministers and received neither. The dictionary records him because he saw the thing the Lord sees and said so: “as sheep having no shepherd” (Mat 9:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compassion as a suffering with another, pity, sympathy; a labourer as one who works, one who performs manual labour; and brutish as stupid, insensible, like a brute.
webster_full: COMPASSION, n. [L. compassio.] A suffering with another; painful sympathy; pity; commiseration.
LABOURER, n. One who labours; one who is employed in coarse work, or in work requiring little skill.
BRUTISH, a. Like a brute or beast; insensible; stupid; unfeeling; savage.
HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering grain; the ripe corn collected; the product of labour.
PLENTEOUS, a. Abundant; copious; plentiful; sufficient for every purpose.
scriptures: Mat 9:36
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
For the pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the LORD: therefore they shall not prosper, and all their flocks shall be scattered.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Meath from 1563 to 1584, whose surveys counted over a hundred roofless parish churches and whose repeated requests for ministers and money were refused.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Brady's letters settle an argument that is still had, and the dictionary cites them for that reason. It is commonly said that the Reformation failed in Ireland because the Irish rejected it. Brady was Irish, Protestant, and in the best-placed diocese in the country, and what he reported year after year was that there was nothing to reject: roofless churches, no preachers, no Irish books, parishes in the hands of men who could not read. The question of Irish receptivity was never put, because the thing that would have put it was never supplied.

The principle to recover is the Lord's own diagnosis of a crowd, which is not that they are hard but that they are unshepherded: “as sheep having no shepherd” (Mat 9:36). His reading of the situation is that the shortage is on the workers' side of the ledger: “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and the first command is to ask the owner of the field for more hands (Mat 9:38). Jeremiah names the failure at the top in one clause, “For the pastors are become brutish, and have not sought the LORD” (Jer 10:21), and the consequence below it follows in the same verse: “therefore they shall not prosper, and all their flocks shall be scattered” (Jer 10:21).

pos: n. (c. 1538–1585; Bishop of Ossory, who set up Irish type and began the Irish New Testament; murdered in his own diocese)
etymology: Walsh, from Old English wealh, a foreigner or Welshman; a name given in Ireland to settlers of Welsh origin.
biblical_def: Nicholas Walsh was the son of a Bishop of Waterford, educated at Oxford and Cambridge, Chancellor of St Patrick's Dublin, and Bishop of Ossory from 1577. With John Kearney he obtained the first fount of Irish type to be used in Ireland and began translating the New Testament into Irish; the work they started was carried forward by Nehemiah Donnellan and completed by Uilliam O Domhnaill, who printed it in 1602. Walsh himself did not live to see it. In 1585 he was stabbed to death in his own house at Kilkenny by a man named James Dullard, whom he had cited before his court for adultery. He was about forty-seven. The dictionary records him because a work handed on unfinished is the ordinary case, and the Lord spoke of it as a law of fruitfulness: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone” (Joh 12:24).

corruption_summary: Bishop of Ossory from 1577, who with John Kearney obtained the first Irish printing type and began the Irish New Testament; stabbed to death in 1585 by a man he had cited for adultery.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is one thing to get straight about how Walsh died, because it is often reported loosely as a sectarian murder. It was not: he was killed by a man he had summoned before the consistory court on a charge of adultery, who stabbed him in his own house. That makes it a different kind of death and in some ways a harder one. He was killed for exercising discipline, which is the part of the ministry that has no admirers and makes enemies one at a time.

The principle to recover is that a work left unfinished at a man's death is not thereby wasted, and that Scripture says so in agricultural terms: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 12:24). Paul's summary of his own life claims a finished course and not a finished programme (2Ti 4:7). The voice from heaven says the works of the dead follow them (Rev 14:13). And Proverbs states what the man who killed him had already risked: “He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed” (Pro 29:1).

pos: n. (c. 1542–c. 1600; treasurer of St Patrick's, who produced the first book ever printed in Irish)
etymology: Kearney, from Irish O Cearnaigh, descendant of the victorious one; cearnach, victorious.
biblical_def: John Kearney was an Irishman who studied at Cambridge, where he was supported by Elizabeth's government as part of a deliberate and short-lived policy of training Irish-speaking Protestant ministers. He returned and became treasurer of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin. In 1571 he brought out Aibidil Gaoidheilge agus Caiticiosma, an Irish alphabet and catechism printed with the fount of Irish type the queen had paid for: the first book ever printed in the Irish language. With Nicholas Walsh he then began the Irish New Testament. The catechism was a small book, and it was the first anything an Irish reader had ever been given in his own letters. The dictionary records him because the command to write a thing down for a later generation is given more than once and plainly: “Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book” (Isa 30:8).

corruption_summary: Treasurer of St Patrick's Dublin, who in 1571 printed Aibidil Gaoidheilge agus Caiticiosma, the first book ever printed in the Irish language.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The date is the thing to notice and it is not creditable to anyone. The first book ever printed in Irish appeared in 1571, nearly forty years after Henry VIII broke with Rome, and it was an alphabet bound to a catechism because the readers it was made for had no letters of their own in print. In those same forty years German, Dutch, French, Swedish, Danish, Welsh, Czech and Polish readers had received Bibles. The Irish got a primer, once, when a queen paid for a single fount of type.

The principle to recover is that God repeatedly commands the committing of his word to writing for people not yet born, and treats the writing as itself an act of obedience. Isaiah is told to do it twice over, on a tablet and in a book: “Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8). Jeremiah is given the same order with a scroll (Jer 36:2), and the scroll is actually produced by a secretary taking dictation (Jer 36:4). Luke undertakes his own orderly writing for the same reason (Luk 1:3).

pos: n. (c. 1570–1628; Uilliam O Domhnaill, who completed the Irish New Testament of 1602 and the Irish Prayer Book of 1608)
etymology: O Domhnaill, from Irish Domhnall, world-mighty; anglicised ODaniel or Daniel.
biblical_def: Uilliam O Domhnaill was one of the first scholars of Trinity College Dublin, a native Irish speaker, and the man who finished the work Nicholas Walsh and John Kearney had begun and Nehemiah Donnellan had carried forward. He completed the translation of the New Testament into Irish and saw it printed in Dublin in 1602 — the first book of Scripture in the Irish language — and followed it in 1608 with the Book of Common Prayer in Irish, so that a congregation could both hear the Scriptures and pray in its own speech. He succeeded Donnellan as Archbishop of Tuam in 1609 and held the see until his death in 1628, nineteen years in the most Irish-speaking province of the country. The dictionary records him for the Pentecost standard he actually met: “because that every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6).

AMEN, adv. [Hebrew.] Verily; truly; so be it; used at the end of prayers to signify assent.

corruption_summary: Native Irish speaker and Trinity scholar who completed the Irish New Testament printed in 1602 and the Irish Prayer Book of 1608; Archbishop of Tuam from 1609 to 1628.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary should be careful not to make O Domhnaill into a solitary hero, and he would have objected to it himself. The 1602 New Testament was the work of a chain of men over a quarter-century: Walsh and Kearney began it and got the type, Donnellan carried it a long way, and O Domhnaill finished it and put it through the press. Attributing a long translation to its last pair of hands is a habit worth breaking, in this case and in others.

The principle to recover is the Pentecost standard, which is not that the gospel be available in a learned tongue but that each man hear it in his own: “because that every man heard them speak in his own language” (Act 2:6). Paul applies the same test to the liturgy and makes the unlearned hearer the judge of it — if he cannot understand the thanksgiving, “how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks” (1Co 14:16). In Christ the distinctions of Greek, Jew, Barbarian and Scythian do not rank the hearers (Col 3:11), and the multitude before the throne is drawn from every tongue (Rev 7:9).
